paragraphs: Rav Chisda (the priest)
(In the Jerusalem Talmud he is sometimes called Chisdai, Chisdi, or Chisdiyy.)[^1]

This great man, who attained Torah, greatness, and length of days, and occupied the seat of Rav and Rav Huna in Sura—nothing at all is known to us about who his forefathers or family were; he is known only by the name “Rav Chisda.”

As for what we find in Sanhedrin 8a, where Rav Nachman bar Yaakov said to Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda, “Thus your father’s father said in the name of Rav,” referring to Rav Chanan bar Rava: Hyman calls this a scribal error there and says it should read “your mother’s father,” as we shall explain below.

When Rav founded his great academy in Sura, Rav Chisda was then two years old. This is explicit in the Epistle of R.Sh.G. [רש״ג], part III, beginning of chapter 2: Rav came to Babylonia in the year 530 of the era of contracts, and Rav Chisda died in 620 of that era, having lived ninety-two years; Rav presided for twenty-eight years. Thus Rav Chisda was two when Rav came to Babylonia and thirty when Rav died. Therefore, without doubt, he still had the privilege of receiving Rav’s teaching from his own mouth.[^2]

This accounts for what we find in Sukkah 33a, Bekhorot 45a, and Niddah 49a: Rav Chisda said, “Our great teacher (Rav) said this; may the Omnipresent be his help.” Likewise, Berakhot 38b has “Rav Chisda expounded in the name of our teacher—and who is that? Rav.” In Beitzah 25a, Rav Chisda said, “From the words of our teacher we shall learn.” (Rashi explains that Rav Huna, Rav Chisda, and Rav Nachman were all students of Rav.) The same is found in Yevamot 110b.

We also find “Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav” in Berakhot 43a, Eruvin 97a, Pesachim 106a, Nazir 43b, Avodah Zarah 31a, 52a, and 60b, and Menachot 17a. Rav’s teachings were so dear to him that he said in Shabbat 10b, “Anyone who comes and tells me a new teaching of Rav’s—I shall give him two gifts from an ox” (for he was a priest).

We likewise find in Shabbat 144b that Rav Chisda said, “From the words of our teacher (Shmuel) we shall learn.” Yet nowhere do we find him speaking face to face with Rav or Shmuel. This is a sign that he did not attain the standing of being counted among Rav’s students.

His principal teacher was Avimi, as he himself said in Arakhin 22a: “I took good blows from Avimi.” In Avodah Zarah 14b he put a difficulty to Avimi because he had not understood the interpretation of the Mishnah, and Avimi explained it to him.

We also find “Rav Chisda said in the name of Avimi” in Sukkah 15a, Ketubot 71b and 106b, Gittin 26b, Sotah 9a, Bava Kamma 93b, Sanhedrin 15a and 81a, Zevachim 26a and 40a, Menachot 27b, and Bekhorot 40b. Menachot 7a asks: “Did Avimi teach Menachot in Rav Chisda’s school? But Rav Chisda said, ‘I took good blows from Avimi’!” It answers that Avimi had forgotten the tractate and came to Rav Chisda so that he would remind him of his learning.

He also received teaching from all the great students of Rav and Shmuel. Thus we find “Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Jeremiah bar Abba” (a student and colleague of Rav) in Berakhot 55b, Taanit 12b, Sanhedrin 103b, and Zevachim 25b; the same should be read in Horayot 6a.

Likewise, “Rav Chisda said in the name of Mar Ukva” (Shmuel’s student, who lived in Kafri) appears in Berakhot 10b and 29a, Shabbat 147b, Eruvin 51a, Pesachim 40a, Ketubot 48a, Gittin 89a, Avodah Zarah 16b, Niddah 52b, and Sanhedrin 70a, where Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Ukva, with an alternative reading “in the name of Mar Ukva.” (Dikdukei Soferim has not even “Rav Ukva.”) In Sotah 39a, Rav Chisda led Mar Ukva along, and he expounded. Yevamot 83b has “Rav Chisda said in the name of Mar Ukva bar Chiyya.”

We likewise find “Rav Chisda said in the name of Zeiri” in Berakhot 43a, Sanhedrin 73a, and Avodah Zarah 31a and 49a. There he says, “Abba bar Chama told me: thus said Zeiri”; at 49a the reading “Abba bar Rav Chisda” is an error.
We also find “Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya” in Menachot 27a.

Likewise, “Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Chanan bar Rava” (Rav’s son-in-law and Rav Chisda’s father-in-law) occurs in Chullin 63a. Pesachim 113a has “Rav Chisda said to the students of the school of Rav Chanan bar Rav,” which, according to Dikdukei Soferim, should read “bar Rava.”

We find Rav Chisda saying in the name of Rabbi Yochanan in Pesachim 116a, Yevamot 25b, Avodah Zarah 27b, and Makkot 23a, and reporting in Rabbi Yochanan’s name in Berakhot 57b. Yet nowhere do we find that Rav Chisda went to the Land of Israel during Rabbi Yochanan’s lifetime. In Berakhot 24b, Rav Huna said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan—and Rav Chisda said to him, “By God, even if Rabbi Yochanan told it to me with his own mouth, I would not heed him.” This implies that he was not his student.

It appears clearly that he received Rabbi Yochanan’s teaching from the travellers who came down from the Land of Israel. Thus, at the end of chapter 4 of the Jerusalem Talmud, Rosh Hashanah, we find Rav Chisda speaking to Rabbi Ze’ira of those “who come down from the West and report there in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.” Perhaps this is why he called Ulla, who was one of these travellers, “our teachers who come down,” in Berakhot 38b: he received the Torah of the Land of Israel from him. In Pesachim 33b we find Rav Chisda saying to Rav Acha bar Rav Avya, “Who heeds you and Rabbi Yochanan, your teacher?”

We also find “Rav Chisda said in the name of R’ Yonatan” in Bava Kamma 66a; according to Dikdukei Soferim, this should read R’ Yochanan. Rav Chisda reports R’ Yitzchak in Sukkah 44b and Chullin 15b, and he asked him questions in Berakhot 27a and 43a.

We likewise find “Rav Chisda said in the name of Ravina bar Shila” in Sukkah 13a, Moed Katan 17b, Yevamot 68b, and Zevachim 69b. (Moed Katan has “Rav Shila,” which should read “Ravina bar Shila,” according to Dikdukei Soferim; Zevachim has “bar Sila,” which should read “bar Shila.”) In Ketubot 75a we find Rav Chisda saying, “I heard this matter from a great man—and who is that? R’ Shila.” It appears that this should read Ravina bar Shila, since R’ Shila died before Rav began to preside. The written form was “Ravi’” [רבי׳], and its stroke and the word bar were lost, producing “R’ Shila.”

We also find “Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Katina” in Bava Metzia 99a, Bekhorot 35a, and Eruvin 32b. He also received teaching from Rav Hamnuna, Rav’s student: Rav Chisda puts a difficulty to him in Horayot, chapter 3, halakhah 6, and in Shabbat 96b Rav Yosef says, “Rav Chisda had a question about this matter, and Rav Hamnuna resolved it for him.”

When Rav Huna began to preside in Sura, Rav Chisda sat before him and became his student and colleague. Rav Chisda was already about forty years old then. (Rav Huna presided for forty years and died in 608 of the era of contracts.) In Berakhot 24b and Pesachim 73a he raises difficulties to Rav Huna; “Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Huna” appears in Pesachim 101a and Beitzah 17a. In Moed Katan Rav Chisda says explicitly, “These things I learned from Rav Huna.”

The reading in Pesachim 100a, “Rav Huna asked Rav Chisda,” is a printing error: it should be the reverse, as in the readings of Bach and Dikdukei Soferim. Bava Metzia 33a relates that Rav Chisda asked Rav Huna about a student whose teacher needs him. Rav Huna suspected that he meant himself, became angry with him, and said, “Chisda, Chisda! I do not need you; you need me.” For forty years they were displeased with each other and did not visit one another. Afterwards Rav Chisda observed forty fasts because he had distressed Rav Huna, and Rav Huna observed forty fasts because he had suspected Rav Chisda.[^8]

Rav Chisda was indeed careful not to issue any ruling in Rav Huna’s place. Eruvin 62b states explicitly that they asked Rav Chisda throughout Rav Huna’s years, and he did not rule. Accordingly, in Bava Metzia 7a, “The incident was in Rav Chisda’s school, and Rav Chisda was in Rav Huna’s school.” Rashi explains that they came before Rav Chisda, and Rav Chisda brought the question before Rav Huna.

His teacher esteemed him greatly. Gittin 7a relates that the exilarch asked Rav Huna where the prohibition of a crown was derived. Rav Huna rose to relieve himself, and Rav Chisda said, “A verse is written.” When Rav Huna returned, he found them studying it, and said, “By God, [it is] rabbinic! But Chisda is your name, and gracious are your words.” In the Jerusalem Talmud, Sotah, chapter 9, at the end of halakhah 15, the account has the exilarch sending a question to R’ Chisdai; R’ Yochanan heard and said, “He is gracious, and his words are gracious.”

In Shabbat 82a, Rav Huna said to his son Rabbah, “Why are you not found before Rav Chisda? His teachings are sharp.” From this we see that he was his student and colleague; Tosafot likewise writes this in Yevamot 83b, under “They say.” Gittin 31b has Rav Huna and Rav Chisda sitting together when Geniva passed them. One said to the other, “Let us stand before him.” The other replied, “Should we stand before a contentious man?” Meanwhile he came over to them, and so on.

It is very plausible that during all the years they were angry with one another, Rav Chisda went to Kafri and issued rulings there. Eruvin 62b says that Rav Chisda ruled in Kafri during Rav Huna’s years. Rashi explains that it was not Rav Huna’s place, his place being Pumbedita—which should read Sura—and that both were in Babylonia. In Bava Metzia 6a, Rav Hoshaya said to Rabbah, “When you go before Rav Chisda in Kafri, ask him.” More likely, however, this was his permanent home; thus he received much teaching from Mar Ukva, who, with his court, was in Kafri, as in Kiddushin 44b. He would go to Sura to study before Rav Huna, then return to his house and issue rulings there.
Disputes between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda occur in Berakhot 25a, Shabbat 146a, Sukkah 3b, Beitzah 14a, Ketubot 24b and 50a, Gittin 24b, Bava Batra 31a, and Chullin 10b.

He was present at Rav Huna’s death. Moed Katan 25a relates that when they wished to place a Torah scroll on his bier, Rav Chisda said, “I learned from him,” and so on. It says there that his coffin was brought up to the Land of Israel, and R’ Abba eulogized him: “Our teacher was worthy of the Divine Presence resting upon him, but Babylonia caused [its absence].” Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda objected—and his father struck him with his sandal. Rashi explains that the father was Rav Chisda. This implies that Rav Chisda too went to the Land of Israel with Rav Huna’s coffin.

This explains what is said in Yevamot 21b: Rav Chisda said, “I heard this matter from a great man—and who was that? R’ Ami.” At the time of his brief visit to the Land of Israel, R’ Ami was academy head in R’ Yochanan’s place, and so he called him a great man. Eruvin 38b says that when Rav Huna died, Rav Chisda entered to set one statement of Rav against another.

With Rav Yehudah, we nowhere find him reporting in his name or speaking with him. Yet in Berakhot 43a Rav Chisda said to R’ Yitzchak, “Rav Yehudah is different, for the Land of Israel is dear to him.” In Chullin 110b he said to Rami bar Tamri, “Had you been in Rav Yehudah’s place, I would have shown you my sharpness.” This implies that he had never been in Rav Yehudah’s place.

His great colleagues were Rav Nachman, Rav Sheshet, and Rabbah bar Rav Huna. Eruvin 67a says that when Rav Chisda met Rav Sheshet, his lips trembled at Rav Sheshet’s Mishnayot—for the Mishnayot were well ordered in his memory, and Rav Chisda feared that he would raise a difficulty against him from a Mishnah, as Rashi explains. Rav Sheshet’s whole body trembled at Rav Chisda’s dialectical sharpness. In Berakhot 49a Rav Chisda said, “I came to the exilarch’s house, and they blessed the Grace after Meals for us”—and Rav Sheshet stiffened against him like a snake.

There, at Berakhot 47b, R’ Ami says that two Torah scholars who sharpen one another in halakhah may count together for a zimmun. Rav Chisda pointed to “such as myself and Rav Sheshet,” while Rav Sheshet pointed to “such as myself and Rav Chisda.” He called him Mar in Gittin 68a, and both travelled together on the road in Berakhot 49a. Rav Sheshet asked him a question in Keritot [כריתות לג.]. Their disputes appear in Eruvin 22b.[^3]

When Rav Chisda came to Rav Huna, he attached himself to his teacher’s son and they studied together. Thus we find “Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna both say” in Shabbat 83a, Pesachim 10b, Ketubot 32b, and Niddah 68b. Both regularly visited the exilarch’s house, as in Sukkah 10b and 26a, and travelled together by boat in Chullin 105b.

At first Rabbah did not wish to go to Rav Chisda. He told his father Rav Huna, in Shabbat 82a, “Why should I go to him? When I go, he seats me with worldly matters. He tells me that one who enters a privy should not sit down hastily or strain excessively, because that muscle rests on three teeth; perhaps the teeth will come loose and he will come into danger.” His father replied, “He is occupied with the life of created beings, and you call it worldly matters? All the more so, go to him!” From then on we find that they studied together continually.

When Rav Nachman came to Sura, he went before Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna in Sukkah 14b; they also appear together in Ketubot 29b, Bava Batra 132b, and Shevuot 38b. In Shabbat 10a, both were sitting in judgment all day and grew faint. Rav Chiyya bar Rav of Difti taught them, “Any judge who renders a judgment in its perfect truth, even for a single hour,” and so on.

We also find Rav Nachman, Rav Chisda, and Rav Sheshet going together to the exilarch’s house in Eruvin 59a. “Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda both say” appears in Bava Metzia 10a and Menachot 31a. Bava Kamma 26b has the message, “Chisda, Chisda! Are you collecting fines in Babylonia?” Rav Chananel also appears in Megillah 18b; see his entry.

Ulla too was his colleague. In Berakhot 58a they were travelling together; when they reached the entrance of Rav Chana bar Chanilai’s house, Rav Chisda groaned. In Taanit 4b Ulla said, “This [teaching] of Rav Chisda is like vinegar to the teeth.” In Berakhot 38b he called Ulla “our teachers who come down,” because Ulla brought the Torah of the Land of Israel to Babylonia, as is well known.

He also disputed with Rav Nachman bar Hoshaya in Yevamot 83a and Chullin 138a. Rav Chisda called Rav Dimi bar Chinana his colleague and brother, as in Zevachim 36a: “It was a familiar saying in the mouth of Rav Dimi bar Chinana.”

Mari bar Mar likewise said, “Rav Chisda said,” in Eruvin 21a and Sanhedrin 17a, and “Mari bar Mar expounded” appears in Gittin 58a; there is a scribal error there. He also disputed with Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi in Sanhedrin 7b, 39a, and 94a, and Menachot 93a. Tosafot there, at 94a, writes that they were colleagues.
He also disputed with R’ Avina in Ketubot 24a. In Shabbat 83a, Avina came and said, “R’ Avina told me.” Rabbah bar Bar Chana also appears in Berakhot 24b.

His halakhic teachings fill the entire Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds. In the latter he is sometimes called Rav Chisdai or Chisdi. In Megillah, chapter 1, R.Ch. [ר״ח] said, “Rav Chisdi—it is R’ Yehudah”; this is what Rav Chisda says in Beitzah 28b. Sotah, chapter 9, at the end of halakhah 15, and Avodah Zarah, chapter 4, halakhah 2, have “The exilarch sent and asked R’ Chisdai,” which is in Gittin 7a; see the entry Rav Chisda. Sanhedrin, chapter 1, halakhah 2, likewise has “Rav Chisdai”; what is said in Sheviit, chapter 10, halakhah 3, and Rosh Hashanah, chapter 2, halakhah 3, is in Rav Chisda’s name. Eruvin, chapter 1, halakhah 4, says, “Abba bar Rav Chana [חנא] said to Rav Chisdai”—and this is Rabbah bar Rav Huna, as is well known.[^2]
His students and those who transmit his sayings:
R’ Ada bar Rav Yitzchak reports Rav Chisda at the end of Menachot.[^4]

Abaye raised a difficulty to Rav Chisda in Taanit 21b. In Zevachim 18a, Abaye said to Rav Chisda’s interpreter, “Ask your master,” and so on. Yoma 77b, however, has the reading that Rav Sheshet said it. R’ Evyatar sent a message to Rav Chisda from the Land of Israel in Gittin 6b.
Rav Oshaya and Rav Chananya lived in his time, as in Bava Metzia 6b. His student Rav Acha bar Huna was sent by him to Rabbah with halakhic rulings, as in Pesachim 40a and Ketubot 89b.

Rav Acha bar Yosef raised a difficulty to Rav Chisda in Bava Metzia 86a and Chullin 105a. Rav Acha bar Rav Avya objected before Rav Chisda, and Rav Chisda said to him, “Who heeds you and Rabbi Yochanan, your teacher?” in Pesachim 33b.
Rav Acha bar Ulla was before Rav Chisda in Shabbat 54b. Rav Achadvoi bar Ami put a contradiction to Rav Chisda in Pesachim 75a.

Rav Idi was before R’ Yosi, reporting in Rav Chisda’s name, in Jerusalem Yevamot, chapter 1, at the end of halakhah 2. Rav Idi bar Avin sat before him in Pesachim 101a. He reports Rav Chisda in Eruvin 59b and Bava Metzia 4a. Rav Chisda said of him, “Is this the man of whom they say that he is a great man?” Rav Chisda called him Mar in Bava Batra 33a.
R’ Ba reports in Rav Chisda’s name in Jerusalem Shabbat, chapter 1, halakhah 1. A Galilean expounded before Rav Chisda in Shabbat 31b, Bava Kamma 92a, Sanhedrin 113a, and Makkot 23a.
Rav Huna bar Chinana sat before him in Moed Katan 9b, and said, “Thus said Rav Chisda,” in Moed Katan 15a. Mar Zutra expounded in his name in Chullin 44b.

R’ Zeira requested of Rav Chisda, “Let the master come and teach,” in Berakhot 49a. R’ Zeira reports Rav Chisda in Beitzah 33b, Ketubot 95a, and Sotah 39a, 39b, and 46b. In the Jerusalem Talmud, R’ Ze’ira reports Rav Chisda in Sheviit, chapter 10, halakhah 2; Shabbat, chapter 7, halakhah 1; Eruvin, chapter 1, halakhah 1, and chapter 5, halakhah 7; Rosh Hashanah, chapter 2, halakhah 1, and chapter 3, halakhah 1; Megillah, chapter 1, halakhah 9; and Nedarim, chapter 6, halakhah 8. The same should be read in Berakhot, chapter 9, halakhah 2, and Sanhedrin, chapter 1, halakhah 4.

R’ Chizkiyah reports in his name in Shekalim, chapter 4, halakhah 4. R’ Chiyya bar Avin asked Rav Chisda a question in Menachot 82a, and said, “An incident took place in Rav Chisda’s school,” in Kiddushin 50a and Bava Metzia 7a. Rav Chiyya bar Ashi reports Rav Chisda in Sanhedrin 82b.

Rav Chiyya, son of Rabbah bar Nachmani, reports Rav Chisda in Berakhot 43a, according to the reading of Dikdukei Soferim; also in Sanhedrin 69b and Avodah Zarah 49b. At Avodah Zarah 31b the text mistakenly reads “the son of R’ Chiyya bar Nachmani.” R’ Chiyya, son of Rav Natan, recited this teaching of Rav Chisda together with him in Pesachim 41a.
Rav Chama raised a difficulty to Rav Chisda in Nazir 20a. Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda objected to Rav Chisda in Shabbat 48a; it appears that he was Rav Chisda’s son, as in Moed Katan 25a.

Rav Chinana reports in his name at the beginning of Maaserot, chapter 1. At the end of Eruvin, chapter 4, R’ Acha says in the name of R’ Chinana, and R’ Chisdiyy—both say. Rav Chanina Vardan objected to Rav Chisda’s words, and Rav Chisda said of him, “Vardan has fallen silent,” in Gittin 60b.

Rav Chinana of Chozai came before Rav Chisda in Moed Katan 2a. R’ Tavi reports in his name in Jerusalem Shabbat, chapter 3, halakhah 4, and Sukkah, chapter 3, at the end of halakhah 1. R’ Yose bar Bun reports in his name at the end of Ketubot, chapter 8.
Rav Yosef called Rav Chisda Mar in Shabbat 96b and Kiddushin 59b. Rav Chisda said to Rav Yosef, “Have you heard this from Rav Yehudah?” in Ketubot 53b.

The Sages sent Rav Yeimar the Elder before Rav Chisda on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, and so on; in the reading of She’iltot his name is R’ Yeiva the Elder. Rav Chisda said to him, “One who lifts damp wood needs its place,” in Eruvin 40b.
R’ Yaakov reports Rav Chisda in Berakhot 29b and Ketubot 60a. Yaakov Chinnana asked Rav Chisda a question in Bava Batra 26b.

Rav Yitzchak bar Ami reports Rav Chisda in Moed Katan 10b and visited Rav Chisda’s house in Shabbat 128a. Rav Menashya bar Gadda reports in his name in Menachot 17a. Mari bar Isak was before him in Bava Metzia 39b. Rav Matna reports Rav Chisda in Kiddushin 32a.

Rabbana Nechemya called Rav Chisda Mar in Bava Batra 51b. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reports Rav Chisda in Avodah Zarah 23a; Dikdukei Soferim reads Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda. Rav Natan bar Abba came before Rav Chisda in Chullin 95b.

Rabbana Ukva called Rav Chisda Mar in Bava Batra 51a. Rav Chisda led Rabbana Ukva along, and he expounded, in Pesachim 115b and Beitzah 29a. Rav Amram asked Rav Chisda a question in Bava Batra 70a. Rav Pappa bar Shmuel sat before him in Shabbat 54b.

His student Rava asked him a question in Kiddushin 53b. Rava said to him, “We expound in your name”; Rav Chisda replied, “May it be [God’s] will that you expound all such fine things in my name,” in Beitzah 28a and Ketubot 68b. Rava raised a difficulty to Rav Chisda in Ketubot 19a. “Rava said in the name of Rav Chisda” appears in Beitzah 17a, Eruvin 103b, Yevamot 74b, Zevachim 13b, and Niddah 40a. In Yoma 75b Rava says explicitly that he was his student. In Sukkah 29a, Rava and Rami bar Chama stood before Rav Chisda, after he had taught them a passage, and quickly ran through the learning, and so on.

Rabbah bar Rav Shila reports Rav Chisda in Shabbat 6a and 39a, Bava Metzia 70a, Chullin 102a, and Menachot 33b; he asked him a question in Shabbat 81a. Rabbah bar Shimi reports Rav Chisda in Chullin 102a, as does Rabbah bar Shmuel in Chullin 102a. Ravin bar Chinana sat before him in Ketubot 53a. Ravina reports Rav Chisda in Pesachim 59a.

Rami bar Chama asked Rav Chisda questions in Eruvin 8a, 34b, and 73a, Pesachim 27b, Zevachim 93a, and Menachot 58a and 86a. Sukkah 29a says explicitly that he was his student. In Bava Kamma 20a, Rav Chisda said to him, “Were you not with us last evening, within the boundary, when we raised fine questions?” Rami bar Chama told him that it was a Mishnah. “Which Mishnah?” he asked. “When you serve me,” he replied. Although he was his student and son-in-law, he knew the source of the law while Rav Chisda did not; he therefore asked him to perform some other service to show that he had learned this law from him. Rav Chisda took his scarf and folded it for him. Rava said of him, “How little the man whom his Master helps feels or is troubled! Even though it was not comparable to the Mishnah, he accepted it from him.”
Rami bar Tamri, who is Rami bar Dikuli of Pumbedita, came to Sura and was brought before Rav Chisda, and so on, in Chullin 110a; see the whole incident there.
Rafram bar Pappa reports Rav Chisda in Berakhot 26a and 53b, Shabbat 81a, Taanit 13a, Ketubot 4a, Kiddushin 81a, Bava Metzia 80b, and Sanhedrin 48a. He interpreted before Rav Chisda in Shabbat 82a.

Rav Shizvi: Shabbat 23b relates that Rav Chisda regularly passed by the entrance to Rav Shizvi’s family home. Seeing that many lamps were regularly kindled there, he said, “A great man will come from here”; Rav Shizvi descended from them. Rav Shizvi reports Rav Chisda in Shabbat 134a, Eruvin 80b, and Yevamot 83a. In Shabbat 143a, Rava says that Rav Shizvi led Rav Chisda astray and he expounded.[^9][^10]

Rav Tachlifa said to Rav Chisda, “Did you not teach us thus, my master?” in the Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, at the beginning of chapter 2. Rav Tachlifa bar Avina was told by Rav Chisda in Chullin 60b, “Go and write of hunters and archers in your aggadah.” Rav Tachlifa bar Maarava lived in his time, as in Eruvin 54b.
He had two students and colleagues who eventually became the great scholars of their generation.

Rav Hamnuna (the third): Rav Chisda praised him to Rav Huna as a great man; he was still unmarried, as in Kiddushin 29b. At 25a, the elders of Nazunia did not come to Rav Chisda’s lecture, and he told Rav Hamnuna, “Go and tell them to stay secluded.” In Nazir 23b Rav Hamnuna asked him a question. Afterwards Rav Hamnuna became his student and colleague, as is explicit in Eruvin 63a, where he ruled in Charta [דארניז?] during Rav Chisda’s years, for he was his student and colleague—this being Rav Hamnuna the third. Their disputes appear in Berakhot 22b, Shabbat 82a, and Eruvin 22b.[^5]

And Rabbah: in Bava Metzia 6a, Rav Hoshaya said to Rabbah, “When you go before Rav Chisda in Kafri, ask him.” Both sat before Rav Huna, as we find in Yevamot 81b, Gittin 26a, and Bava Metzia 18b. Rav Chisda said to Rabbah, “Go and look carefully at it, for Rav Huna will ask you about it tonight.” In Nedarim 89a he said to Rabbah, “Who heeds you and Rav Huna, your teacher?” In Bava Kamma 89a he said of Rabbah, “Master of the law.” Throughout Rav Chisda’s years of rule, Rabbah did not wish to accept the office at Pumbedita, as we shall explain below.
Incidents of his long life, his piety, his rise to greatness, and his wealth.

We have already written above that nowhere do we find who his forefathers or family were. We do know, however, that he was a priest, as is explicit in Berakhot 44a, Shabbat [ו:], and Chullin 44b. While he was still a youth, Rav Chisda relates that a Chaldean told him, “You will be a teacher”—that is, you will be a sage—in Yevamot 21a.[^6]

His devotion to Torah was astonishing. He would study all night, as in Eruvin 65a. Once his daughter said to him, “Does the master not wish to sleep a little?” He answered her, “Now the days that are long and short will come, and we shall sleep much.” He married at sixteen, as he himself says in Kiddushin 29b: “The reason I am superior to my colleagues is that I married at sixteen. Had I married at fourteen, I would have said to Satan, ‘An arrow in your eye!’”

Whose daughter was his wife? It appears that when Rav Chisda was a young student listening in Rav’s academy, Rav Chanan bar Rava, Rav’s son-in-law, saw that blessing was upon him and gave him his daughter as a wife; he thus acquired Rav’s granddaughter for him. This is explicit in Kiddushin 77b, where Rav Chisda said to his son Rav Chanan, “Thus your mother’s father said in the name of Rav”; it says there, “Rav Chanan bar Rava said in the name of Rav.” In Kiddushin 81b the reading “Rav Acha bar Abba” is an error. Likewise, in Sanhedrin 8a, “your father’s father” is an error and should read “your mother’s father.”[^9]

He was very poor. As he himself said in Shabbat 140b, when he was poor he did not eat vegetables, because they draw the appetite and he would need to eat much bread, which he did not have. Afterwards he began making beer, and the Lord sent him success; from this he became very wealthy. In Pesachim 113a Rav Chisda says, “Had I not put beer to ferment, I would not have become wealthy.” Even then he did not eat vegetables, saying in Shabbat 140b, “Where vegetables enter, let meat and fish enter.”

His wealth did not make his heart proud, so that he would say, “My strength and the might of my hand made me all this wealth.” Rather, in Shabbat 62b he said, “I wash with hands full of water, and they give me hands full of goodness.” He himself sliced beets—he cut the produce in honor of the Sabbath—as in Shabbat 119a. He greeted every person first, even gentiles, in Gittin 62a. Once, when he unintentionally distressed his teacher Rav Huna, he fasted forty fasts, as is explicit in Bava Metzia 33b.[^8]

His name grew so great that it reached R’ Yochanan in the Land of Israel, who said of him, “He is gracious, and his words are gracious,” in Jerusalem Sotah, chapter 9, at the end of halakhah 15. He was among the pious men of Babylonia, as is explicit in Taanit 23b. Already during Rav Huna’s lifetime he was head in Kafri and issued rulings there, as is explicit in Eruvin 62b. According to the testimony of Rava, who later became his son-in-law, the Lord always heard his prayer when he prayed for rain, in Moed Katan 28a.
A miraculous incident is related of him: quails were found among his logs, in Yoma 75b. His wealth grew so great that even his dogs ate fine flour in abundance, as in Moed Katan 28a.

His wife bore him fine sons: Rav Chanan, whom, without doubt, they named after his father-in-law, as in Moed Katan 25a; Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda, in Berakhot 21a, who expounded in his name in Shabbat 147a—Tosafot in Bava Batra 141a likewise writes that he was his son. We also find Rav Shimi, Rav Mari, and Rav Pinchas, sons of Rav Chisda, in Bava Kamma 110a. Mar Yanuka and Mar Kashisha, sons of Rav Chisda, however, appear not to have been sons of this Rav Chisda, as explained in their entries. Rav Tachlifa bar Rav Chisda appears in Gittin 31b.[^9]

She also bore him daughters, and Rav Chisda watched over them carefully, teaching them modesty. In Shabbat 140b he said, “Be modest before your husbands.” He also taught them never to let any falsehood leave their mouths. Rava testifies in Ketubot 85a concerning Rav Chisda’s daughter, “I know that she does not lie.”[^7]

He had already betrothed his daughter while she was still a child. Kiddushin 81b relates that his father-in-law came, took his granddaughter, and seated her in his lap. Rav Chisda said to him, “Does the master not hold that she is betrothed [and it is forbidden]?” He answered, “You have transgressed Rav’s teaching”—for it is forbidden to betroth one’s daughter while she is a minor. Two of his daughters married two of the great men of the generation, Rami bar Chama and Mar Ukva bar Chama, as in Berakhot 44a.

Of Rami bar Chama’s wife, Bava Batra 12b relates that she was sitting in her father’s lap when she was little, while Rava and Rami bar Chama sat before him. Her father asked, “Which of them do you want?” She answered, “Both.” Rava said, “And I shall be last.” So it happened, as explained in Berakhot 56a and Yevamot 34b.

His wife used to adorn herself before her daughter-in-law. Rav Chisda said of this, “This is what people say: a woman of sixty runs like a girl of six at the sound of a drum,” in Moed Katan 9b. Since he attained a long life, it is no wonder that Rava said in Moed Katan 28a that Rav Chisda lived to see sixty weddings. This is no exaggeration. (The scholar Sh.I.R. [שי״ר], in his translation of the scholar Graetz’s works, volume II, page 300, mistakenly copied eighty.)[^2]
His daughters were so dear to him that in Bava Batra 141a he said, “For me, daughters are preferable to sons.” This was because they married the great men of the generation.

Although he had many attendants and slaves, as befitted so wealthy a man, we nevertheless find that he personally looked after his property and orchards. In Bava Kamma 91b, when he walked among thorns and shrubs, he lifted his clothes, saying, “This heals, but this does not heal.” At 92a, Rav Chisda saw palms among vines and told his tenant, “Uproot them: vines can buy palms, but palms cannot buy vines.” Gittin 56a says that he entrusted all his keys to his attendant, except those for the firewood.

Seder HaDorot explains well that he always found the wood there. Lest one say that this was why he did not entrust him with the key, it says there that Rav Chisda said, “For a wheat storehouse, sixty wood storehouses are needed.”

He was also highly expert in the nature of animals. In Nazir 31b he said, “Black among white is poor; black for its hide, red for its flesh, white for ploughing.” From this too we see that he kept a watchful eye on all his property.

His precious sayings in Shabbat 140b show the same: “A scholar who buys vegetables should buy a long bundle: one bundle is like another, and the extra length comes of itself. One who can eat barley bread but eats wheat bread transgresses ‘Do not destroy.’ A scholar who buys meat should buy the neck, for it contains three kinds of meat. A scholar who buys a shirt should buy from Nehar Abba and wash it every thirty days; it will suffice for him for twelve months of the year, and I guarantee it. A scholar should not sit on a new mat, which wears out his clothes. A scholar should not send his clothes to his host to wash: it is not proper conduct, lest he see something on them and come to despise him.” From this we see his love and affection for his students.

According to the testimony of R.Sh.G. [רש״ג], part III, at the end of chapter 4, in the year 604 of the era of contracts—that is, when Rav Chisda was seventy-six—he built the house of Rav during Rav Huna’s lifetime. Without doubt, the meaning is that he built it with his own money in Sura. Thus, in Sanhedrin 17b we find “the elders of Sura, Rav Huna and Rav Chisda.” They were in fact almost the same age. Rav Huna reached the age of strength, as is explicit in Moed Katan 28a, and died in 608; Rav Chisda too was then about eighty, unless we say that Rav Huna lived beyond eighty. The meaning of “Rav Huna reached the age of strength” is that eighty years had passed over him.[^2]

When Rav Huna died and his coffin was brought to the Land of Israel, Rashi’s explanation in Moed Katan 25a, under “He struck him,” implies that Rav Chisda too came to the Land of Israel to accompany Rav Huna. It is very difficult to say that an eighty-year-old would then go up to the Land of Israel.

When Rav Huna died, the whole academy came to Rav Yehudah in Pumbedita. That is, no head of the academy was appointed in Sura during Rav Yehudah’s lifetime. Rav Chisda, apparently, did not go there, but spread Torah in Sura. Only in 610 of the era of contracts, two years after Rav Huna, when Rav Yehudah died, was Rav Chisda installed as academy head in Sura, while Rabbah was installed in Pumbedita, since Rav Yosef did not wish to accept the office. Yet Rabbah too did not conduct himself as academy head until the end of Rav Chisda’s days. All this is explained in the Epistle of R.Sh.G., part III, beginning of chapter 3.[^2]

This is explained in Eruvin 43a: “Those seven teachings that were said on Sabbath morning before Rav Chisda in Sura were said towards evening on the Sabbath before Rabbah in Pumbedita.” Kiddushin 12b likewise tells of a man who betrothed a woman with a blue stone: Rav Chisda sat assessing its value—and some of that family remained in Sura, and so on. In Chullin 110a, Rami bar Tamri came to Sura on the eve of Yom Kippur, ate udder, and was brought before Rav Chisda.

When he signed, he did not sign his name, but drew a samekh, as in Gittin 36a and Bava Batra 161b. He presided for ten years and died in 620 of the era of contracts, as is explicit in the Epistle of R.Sh.G., part III, at the end of chapter 2.[^2]

Makkot 10a relates his death: the angel of death could not overcome him, because his mouth did not cease from his learning. [The angel] went up and sat in the cedar of the academy; the cedar split, Rav Chisda fell silent, and the angel could overcome him. He was then ninety-two years old.

In Moed Katan 25a they wished to place a Torah scroll on his bier, saying, “This man fulfilled what is written in this.” Rabbi Yitzchak—in Seder HaDorot, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ami, his student—prevented them: “Something of which his teacher did not approve—shall we rise and do it for him?” They thought they should not stitch up their torn garments, but Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ami said, “For a sage, once they have turned their faces away,” and so on.

Rava was not present at his death. Yoma 75b says that Rava’s tenant used to bring him quail every day. One day he did not bring it, and Rava asked, “What is this?” He went up to the roof and heard a child saying, “I heard, and my belly trembled.” He said, “It follows that Rav Chisda has died, and for the great teacher’s sake the student eats.” In Rav Chisda’s merit Rava ate, and now that he had died, the quail ceased.
No head of the academy was appointed in Sura after his death, although Torah continued to be taught there, until Rav Ashi was appointed.

notes.text: This translation presents Hyman’s account. His proposed emendations, identifications, reconstructions of family relationships, and judgments about earlier writers remain his arguments; they do not establish those conclusions independently.
The initials R.Sh.G. (רש״ג), R.Ch. (ר״ח), and Sh.I.R. (שי״ר) are retained where their full form has not been established in this review.
Hyman’s citation is printed כריתות לג. It is retained here without a conjectural replacement.
Hyman prints R’ Ada bar Rav Yitzchak. The consulted text of Menachot 110a instead reads Rabbi Abba bar Rav Yitzchak. The translation retains Hyman’s name.

The bracketed Hebrew after Charta is a tentative reading because its printed letterform remains uncertain. The consulted text of Eruvin 63a reads בחרתא דארגז. Hyman’s later citation עירובין כב: is retained without silently substituting another folio.
The citation שבת ו: follows the printed entry and remains unresolved here.
“I know that she does not lie” follows Hyman’s explanatory wording. The consulted passage in Ketubot 85a says that Rava knew her reliability (קים לי בגווה).

The account of forty years and the two sets of forty fasts follows Hyman’s presentation. In the consulted text of Bava Metzia 33a, “forty years” occurs in Rav Huna’s reply. Hyman’s later citation of Bava Metzia 33b for the fasts is retained; the passage consulted here is on 33a.
The citations Shabbat 143a, Kiddushin 77b, and Bava Kamma 110a follow Hyman. The stated material was not located in the consulted texts of those pages; no replacement citation is supplied here.
Rashi on Shabbat 23b explains the household as that of Rav Shizvi’s father, with an alternative explanation referring to his father-in-law. “Family home” leaves that distinction open.
